p1.key: A free radical has an unpaired electron and forms when a covalent bond breaks homolytically, with each atom taking one electron. Heterolytic fission produces ions.
UV light splits Cl<sub>2</sub> by homolytic fission into Cl• radicals, which take part in free-radical substitution. No ions are formed.
A radical has an unpaired electron (not a lone pair), is formed by homolytic fission in which each atom keeps one electron, and is usually uncharged.
A free radical has an unpaired electron, shown by a dot: •CH<sub>3</sub>. ⁺CH<sub>3</sub> is a carbocation, ⁻CH<sub>3</sub> and :CH<sub>3</sub> carry a lone pair (carbanion).
Alkanes are unreactive towards ions but react with radicals. The bromine radical Br• abstracts H from propane in the propagation step of free-radical substitution.
Alkanes react with halogens in UV light by free-radical substitution: C2H6 + Br2 → C2H5Br + HBr. B is electrophilic addition; C and D are nucleophilic substitutions. A.
I: Cl replaces H in propane using Cl<sub>2</sub>/UV, a free-radical substitution. II: OH⁻ replaces Cl in 1-chloropropane, a nucleophilic substitution. No oxidation occurs.

I and II are propagation steps: Br• takes an H atom, then C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• takes a Br from Br<sub>2</sub>, regenerating Br•. III, where two radicals combine, is a termination step. All three occur in the mechanism.

A propagation step uses up one radical and makes another: Cl• + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>• + HCl. C is initiation and D is termination. B is wrong because Cl• takes an H atom; it does not replace one directly.
A propagation step uses one radical and makes another: CH<sub>4</sub> + Br• → •CH<sub>3</sub> + HBr. D is termination (two radicals combine); A and C do not occur.
UV light causes homolytic fission of the weakest bond, C–Cl (weaker than C–F), giving two radicals: CCl2F2 → •CClF2 + •Cl. Ions (heterolytic fission) are not formed.
O2 needs shorter-wavelength (242 nm) radiation, which carries more energy per photon, to break its bond, so the O=O bond in O2 needs more energy to break than the bonds in O3 (340 nm).
Alkanes react with halogens by free-radical substitution. UV light splits the halogen molecule evenly, one electron to each atom: homolytic fission.

In sunlight (UV), Cl2 splits homolytically into Cl• radicals, which substitute an H on methane in a chain reaction: free-radical substitution. Alkanes are non-polar, so they do not react with electrophiles or nucleophiles.

A propagation step uses one radical and makes a new one: •C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + •Cl. A is initiation, C is termination; D is wrong because it forms an H radical (H is removed as HCl).

p1.key: CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> (in UV) is free-radical substitution, which starts with homolytic fission of Cl<sub>2</sub>. B and C are nucleophilic substitutions and D is electrophilic substitution, which involve heterolytic fission.
The bonds in O3 (bond order 1.5) are weaker than the O=O double bond in O2, so less energy is needed: lower energy light, i.e. longer wavelength (E = hc/λ).
